clinicalPearls: In children and adolescents obesity is defined using body mass index relative to age- and sex-specific percentiles rather than fixed adult cut-offs, with obesity typically at or above the 95th percentile.
The vast majority of cases are related to lifestyle and energy balance; a monogenic or endocrine cause is uncommon but should be considered in specific circumstances.
A tall child growing well who is obese is usually exogenously obese, whereas an obese child who is short or growing poorly raises suspicion of an endocrine or syndromic cause.
Ask about diet, physical activity, screen time, sleep, family history, and psychosocial factors, as these shape both cause and management.
Screen for comorbidities including type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease, and obstructive sleep apnoea.
Acanthosis nigricans is a clinical clue to insulin resistance and increased type 2 diabetes risk.
Management centres on sustainable family-based lifestyle change addressing nutrition, activity, sleep, and behaviour rather than short-term restrictive dieting.
Early-onset severe obesity, particularly with hyperphagia, may suggest a monogenic cause and warrants specialist evaluation.
reference.pathophysiology: Childhood obesity results from a chronic positive energy balance in which caloric intake exceeds expenditure, leading to excess adipose tissue. This arises from a complex interplay of genetic susceptibility, dietary patterns, physical inactivity, sleep, and environmental and socioeconomic influences. Expanded and dysfunctional adipose tissue drives insulin resistance, low-grade inflammation, and altered adipokine signalling, which underlie the associated metabolic, hepatic, cardiovascular, and endocrine complications. Rare monogenic and syndromic disorders disrupt central appetite regulation (notably the leptin-melanocortin pathway).
additionalDifferentials: Monogenic obesity (e.g. leptin or MC4R pathway defects)
Hypothalamic obesity (e.g. after CNS tumour or its treatment)
additionalInvestigations: BMI plotted on age- and sex-specific percentile charts, with blood pressure measurement
Fasting glucose and/or HbA1c and fasting lipid profile
Liver function tests and assessment for fatty liver disease
Thyroid function testing where clinically indicated
Evaluation for obstructive sleep apnoea when symptoms suggest it
Genetic or endocrine work-up for early-onset severe or syndromic obesity
redFlags: Obesity combined with poor linear growth or short stature suggesting an endocrine cause
Symptoms of type 2 diabetes such as polyuria, polydipsia, or an incidental very high glucose
Signs of obstructive sleep apnoea including loud snoring, apnoeic pauses, or daytime somnolence
Features of Cushing syndrome (central obesity, striae, hypertension, growth deceleration)
Early-onset severe obesity with extreme hyperphagia suggesting a monogenic disorder
Hip or knee pain suggesting a slipped capital femoral epiphysis
reference.prognosis: Childhood obesity frequently persists into adulthood and raises the long-term risk of type 2 diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and other complications; early sustained family-based lifestyle intervention can improve trajectory and reduce comorbidity.
pitfalls: Assuming all obesity is lifestyle-related and missing an endocrine, syndromic, or monogenic cause when growth is impaired
Failing to screen for comorbidities such as type 2 diabetes, fatty liver, and sleep apnoea
Focusing on the child alone rather than engaging the whole family in change
Overlooking psychosocial factors, stigma, and mental health in management
management: Family-based lifestyle intervention is the foundation, combining dietary change with reduced energy-dense foods, increased physical activity, less screen time and improved sleep
Behavioural and psychological support that addresses eating behaviour and psychosocial contributors
Screen for and manage comorbidities including type 2 diabetes, dyslipidaemia, hypertension, non-alcoholic fatty liver disease and obstructive sleep apnoea
Pharmacotherapy such as a GLP-1 receptor agonist or orlistat in selected adolescents with severe obesity or significant comorbidity, alongside lifestyle measures
Bariatric surgery in carefully selected adolescents with severe obesity and complications
Investigate for a monogenic, endocrine or syndromic cause where obesity is early-onset and severe or accompanied by short stature or poor growth
Referral to a specialist multidisciplinary weight-management service
Regular monitoring of BMI percentile, blood pressure and metabolic parameters to track response
